questions.q: Which of these best defines data governance as used in this course?
options: The system of decision rights, accountability, and rules over how data is created, accessed, and used
A specific software tool for managing databases
The IT department responsible for server uptime
A one-time project to clean up a spreadsheet
questions.explain: Governance is a system of agreements and accountability, not a tool or a single team â€” the lesson's core definition.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the first of the four tests a real asset must pass?
options: It has an identifiable, named owner
It must be stored in a cloud database
It must appear in a press release
It must be used by every department
questions.explain: The four tests are ownership, measurable value, active maintenance, and being weighed in decisions â€” ownership is the first.

questions.q: Which question does data governance answer, per the lesson?
options: Who decides, and what's the rule?
Is this specific dataset correct right now?
How do we physically store this data?
Which cloud vendor should we use?
questions.explain: Governance is the rulebook â€” who decides and what the policy is. Management is the day-to-day doing; quality is the measurable scorecard.

questions.q: How does the lesson say governance programs typically fail?
options: Quietly â€” budget keeps renewing and meetings continue while the underlying problems never go away
With a sudden, dramatic, visible collapse
Only when the company goes bankrupt
They never fail once funded
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes that failure is usually quiet and ongoing, not a dramatic visible event â€” which makes it harder to notice early.

questions.q: In the DAMA Wheel, what sits at the center?
options: Data Governance
Data Quality
Metadata Management
Data Warehousing and Business Intelligence
questions.explain: Data Governance sits at the hub, with the other ten knowledge areas arranged as spokes around it, since governance underpins all of them.

questions.q: What is COBIT primarily, and how does data governance fit into it?
options: An IT governance framework (maintained by ISACA) with data governance as one component inside a larger scope
A data-governance-only framework with no connection to IT
A regulatory law requiring data breach notification
A certification exam for data stewards
questions.explain: COBIT covers the full scope of enterprise IT governance; data governance is one piece inside that broader framework, not its sole focus.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a framework and an operating model, per the lesson?
options: A framework defines what needs to be governed; an operating model defines who governs it and how, day to day
They are two names for exactly the same thing
A framework only applies to small companies; an operating model only applies to large ones
An operating model is a piece of software; a framework is a document
questions.explain: DMBOK (a framework) defines what needs governing â€” the operating model defines who does the governing and where authority sits.

questions.q: How does a federated model split responsibility, per the lesson?
options: A central body governs shared/cross-cutting data and standards; business units keep authority over their own local data
Everything is governed centrally, with no local authority at all
Everything is governed locally, with no shared standards at all
Governance authority rotates randomly between departments each quarter
questions.explain: Federated governance deliberately splits the difference: central standards for what needs consistency, local authority for everything else.

questions.q: According to DAMA-DMBOK, what is a data owner?
options: The individual responsible for definition, policy, and practice decisions about data within their area of responsibility
The database administrator who maintains the system storing the data
Any employee who regularly uses the data in their job
The vendor that sells the data storage platform
questions.explain: DAMA-DMBOK's definition centers on approval authority and accountability within a business domain, not on who technically maintains the system.

questions.q: How does DAMA-DMBOK define a data steward?
options: A business leader and/or subject matter expert accountable for tasks related to data management
The executive who funds the governance program
A piece of software that automatically cleans data
Anyone with read access to a database
questions.explain: DAMA-DMBOK ties stewardship to tasks related to data management, held by someone with business or subject-matter expertise.

questions.q: What does the 'A' in RACI stand for, and what does it mean?
options: Accountable â€” owns the outcome, with final sign-off authority
Approved â€” a task that has already finished
Assigned â€” anyone who was given the task on a list
Advisory â€” someone who can be ignored safely
questions.explain: Accountable means owning the outcome and having final sign-off; there should be exactly one Accountable party per task.

questions.q: What is the key difference between initial sponsorship and sustained sponsorship?
options: Sustained sponsorship means ongoing, renewed backing over time, not a one-time approval
There is no real difference between the two
Initial sponsorship always lasts longer than sustained sponsorship
Sustained sponsorship means the sponsor no longer needs to be named publicly
questions.explain: Getting an initial yes is the easy part; programs stall when that backing quietly erodes instead of being renewed each cycle.

questions.q: What level does a data policy operate at?
options: High-level vision and direction â€” what is required and why, not how to implement it
The exact technical configuration of a database table
A single employee's personal task list
The precise encryption algorithm an application must use
questions.explain: Policies state the rule and reasoning; the implementation detail belongs to standards, covered in the next lesson.

questions.q: How does a data standard differ from a data policy?
options: A standard provides the concrete, technical detail that implements the policy's high-level requirement
A standard and a policy are exactly the same thing with different names
A standard always overrides and replaces its related policy
Only executives are allowed to read standards, while anyone can read a policy
questions.explain: The policy states what is required and why; the standard specifies the exact, checkable rule that implements it.

questions.q: Which of these correctly lists the six policy lifecycle stages in order, per this lesson?
options: Drafting, review, approval, publication, review and revision, retirement
Publication, retirement, drafting, approval, review, revision
Approval, drafting, retirement, review, publication, revision
Retirement, drafting, publication, review, approval, revision
questions.explain: The lifecycle runs drafting through review, approval, publication, scheduled review/revision, and finally retirement.

questions.q: Which of these best describes GDPR's scope and consent model?
options: Applies globally to processing EU residents' personal data; generally requires opt-in consent
Applies only to California residents; uses an opt-out model
Applies only to US healthcare providers
Has no consent requirements of any kind
questions.explain: GDPR applies based on whose data is processed (EU residents), regardless of where the processing organization is based, and generally requires opt-in consent.

questions.q: What is the most common reason a data governance program stalls in its first year, according to this lesson?
options: A readiness gap â€” missing sponsorship, capacity, or business agreement â€” not a lack of technology
The catalog tool chosen was the wrong vendor
The program moved too slowly through its roadmap phases
There were too many data stewards assigned
questions.explain: Teams often buy tooling and write a charter while skipping the readiness check â€” the real gap is almost always sponsorship, capacity, or business agreement, not the technology.

questions.q: What are the four components of a credible business case described in this lesson?
options: The problem in business terms, the proposed solution and scope, required resources, and anticipated value with a way to measure it
A maturity model, an operating model, a RACI chart, and a policy library
A vendor comparison, a budget forecast, a staffing plan, and a risk register
A mission statement, a vision statement, a charter, and a council roster
questions.explain: The four components are: the problem framed in business terms, the proposed solution and its scope, the resources required, and the anticipated value along with how it will be measured.

questions.q: What are the three criteria for choosing a good pilot domain?
options: High value, high pain, and high feasibility
Low cost, low risk, and low visibility
High complexity, high headcount, and high regulatory exposure
Executive preference, vendor availability, and tooling maturity
questions.explain: The best pilot domain scores well on all three: it matters to the business (value), people already feel the problem (pain), and a small team can actually finish within a defined window (feasibility).

questions.q: What is a governance roadmap's relationship to a pilot, according to this lesson?
options: The roadmap sequences the work in phases, with the pilot as one phase, rather than repeating the pilot in every domain at once
The roadmap replaces the need for a pilot entirely
The roadmap and the pilot are unrelated documents created by different teams
The roadmap must be completed before a pilot can be scoped
questions.explain: A roadmap turns a single pilot's proof point into an organization-wide program by sequencing phases â€” discovery, foundation, the pilot itself, expand, and scale â€” rather than running the pilot everywhere simultaneously.
